Here's how Canadians can avoid a costly 1-hour mix-up
 Amy Tokic and Romana King Sun, October 18, 2026 at 5:00 a.m. EDT 7 min read Daylight Savings Time It's 12pm — lunchtime in Toronto — and you click a meeting link for that important business meeting or job interview. Only no one is in the call. You check your email only to realize you've missed three urgent requests asking you to join the call. What happened? 
 For many Canadians calculating the time difference between major Canadian (or North American) cities is common practice. Everyone knows there's a three-hour difference between Toronto and Vancouver. But that changes as of Nov. 1. 
 "Don't assume you know the time elsewhere in Canada. Check before you call, travel or schedule an online meeting," explains Kim MacDonald of The Weather Network in an interview with Money.ca.

 As of this year, a few provinces and territories have opted out of the fall back / spring forward cycle of daylight savings. 
 To help, here's what you need to know about the new rules of daylight saving time; how this impacts Canadians and what you'll need to remember when travelling, working or communicating with someone in another part of Canada. 
 The provinces sticking with fall back / spring forward or no change 
 For most of Ontario, the clocks will continue to roll back on Nov. 1. That means residents in Toronto, Ottawa, and Thunder Bay — all in the Eastern Time Zone (ET) — will continue to adjust their clocks: rolling back an hour on Nov. 1 and springing forward an hour in 2027. 
 Saskatchewan residents will also remain true to their time zone — meaning no fall back or spring forward. This isn't a change but a continuation of what's always been done as the province continues to use Central Standard Time (CST). Turns out provinces (and U.S. states) on CST do not alter the clocks throughout the year. 
 For residents in Atlantic Canada, which includes New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador, the clocks will fall back this year. So, no change for Atlantic coast provinces. 
 The same applies to residents in Nunavet, Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Quebec. 
 For Yukon residents, none of this is new. The territory elected to stop changing its clocks in 2020 and its observed Yukon Standard Time (YST) year-round. 
 Quebec is a tad more complicated, despite a lack of change. This province has two different time zones : 
 Story Continues Most of Quebec, including Montreal, Quebec City, Gatineau, Sherbrooke, Trois-Rivières and Saguenay, follows daylight saving time and will turn clocks back one hour on Nov. 1. 
 The Lower North Shore (Basse-Côte-Nord), in the Côte-Nord administrative region, follows Atlantic Standard Time (AST) year-round and will not change its clocks. 
 As a result, at 2am on Nov. 1, most of Quebec will move its clocks back to 1am — switching from Eastern Daylight Time (EDT) to Eastern Standard Time (EST). The Lower North Shore will remain on AST, so residents in the Lower North Shore will go from being on the same clock time as Montreal during the summer to being one hour ahead during the winter.

 Regions that are changing their approach to daylight savings time 
 As of this year, there are a number of provinces and regions that are adjusting their approach to daylight savings time. 
 Northern Ontario 
 Communities west of the 90th meridian (such as Kenora and Atikokan) will not shift their clocks this fall — so no fall rollback for the clocks on Nov. 1. This means Northern Ontario residents will stay aligned with Manitoba, when it comes to the time. 
 Manitoba 
 Manitoba announced on Sept. 17, 2026 , that it is adopting permanent daylight saving time. As a result, Manitoba residents will not turn its clocks back on Nov. 1, 2026. Instead, the province will remain on Daylight Saving Time (DST) starting Nov. 1, 2026 and stop all subsequent seasonal adjustments. 
 A surprising consequence 
 Starting Nov. 1, Winnipeg and Toronto will have the same local time for the winter, even though Winnipeg has traditionally been one hour behind Toronto. 
 For example, when it's 9 a.m. in Toronto on Nov. 2, it will also be 9 a.m. in Winnipeg. Before Nov. 1, it would have been 8 a.m. in Winnipeg. 
 The two cities will return to being one hour apart when Ontario moves its clocks forward in March 2027. 
 Alberta 
 Alberta is changing by adopting permanent Alberta Time (ABT) , what is equivalent Mountain Daylight Time (MDT). 
 The province passed legislation in May 2026 and ABT will take effect on Nov. 1, when the province will not roll back clocks and officially end the fall/spring clock change. 
 An interesting consequence is that Alberta will be two hours behind Toronto and other EDT regions during the summer and only one hour behind during the winter months. 
 British Columbia 
 B.C. adopted permanent daylight saving time after its final clock change in March 2026. The province's new time zone will be called Pacific Time (PCT). This means Vancouver and Whitehorse will continue sharing the same local time throughout the year; however, anyone crossing into the U.S. will need to adjust their clocks, as the states of Washington and Oregon as well as California still roll back their clocks. 
 From Nov. 1, 2026 until March 14, 2027, Vancouver and other B.C. cities will be one hour ahead of U.S. cities on west coast, until those U.S. states spring forward — effectively creating a new time difference between Vancouver and major U.S. west coast cities. 
 What this means for travellers, businesses and the rest of Canada 
 "Canadians are used to springing forward and falling back together, but that's changing," says MacDonald. "Some provinces are keeping their summer time year-round, while others will still change their clocks. That means familiar time differences may shift, or disappear altogether." 
 Winnipeggers will now eat lunch at the same time as Torontonians. In B.C., a customer service line that opens at 9am EST now opens at 7am local time, not 6am. Western investors will see the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) open at 7:30am in Vancouver and 8:30 am in Calgary, an hour later than last winter. 
 And companies are also warning customers to check and confirm calendar times. For instance, Microsoft has warned that people using Outlook may need to update their time-zone settings and review recurring meetings and appointments scheduled beyond Nov. 1 to prevent calendar errors. 
 Need a cheatsheet for scheduling around these time zone changes? 
 To wrap your head around the possible or actual changes, here's a snapshot of the major changes for Canadians: 
 Vancouver and Toronto: The time difference shrinks from three hours to two. 
 Calgary and Toronto: The difference shrinks from two hours to one. 
 Winnipeg and Toronto: Both cities will have the same time during winter. 
 Vancouver and Calgary: They remain one hour apart. 
 Toronto and Halifax: They remain one hour apart.
